ideas.title: Every Model Lab Is Now a Supplier to OpenRouter
ideas.trend: OpenRouter raised $113M Series B on May 26 led by CapitalG (Google's growth fund) with NVIDIA, ServiceNow, MongoDB, Snowflake, Databricks, a16z, and Menlo Ventures also investing; weekly token volume hit 25 trillion — up 5x in six months — valuation doubled to $1.3B in one year
ideas.consensus: OpenRouter is an enterprise AI infrastructure play betting on multi-model adoption as companies avoid single-vendor lock-in
ideas.angle: Every investor in OpenRouter should logically want it to fail: Google funds a router that makes Gemini interchangeable, NVIDIA funds optimization away from raw compute, enterprise software vendors fund the infrastructure that routes their customers away from any single product. They all invested because the enterprise market already decided it will not commit to one model. The model competition is OpenRouter's supply chain, not its threat.

content_pack.x_longform:
OpenRouter just raised $113 million from the companies that should want it to fail.

CapitalG led the round. That is Alphabet's independent growth fund. Google's own model, Gemini, is one of 400 options in OpenRouter's catalog. Every enterprise routing through OpenRouter can pick Gemini or Claude or GPT-5.5 or DeepSeek on each individual query. The router has no loyalty to any provider.

Also on the cap table: NVentures (NVIDIA), ServiceNow Ventures, MongoDB Ventures, Snowflake Ventures, Databricks Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, Menlo Ventures.

Read that list again. That is the backbone of the enterprise software stack. Every one of those investors profits when enterprises build deep, sticky integrations with a single AI provider. They all funded the infrastructure that removes that stickiness.

The numbers behind the bet: 25 trillion tokens routed per week. Up 5 times in the last six months. Over a quadrillion tokens a year, per Menlo Ventures. Valuation $1.3 billion post-money, up from $547 million twelve months ago. In one year, the routing layer doubled in value. The frontier model labs did not.

OpenRouter sits between enterprise buyers and more than 400 model providers. A query comes in. The platform routes it to whichever model is cheapest, fastest, or most accurate on the specific parameters that request demands. The enterprise does not commit to a winner. The router optimizes continuously.

That architecture is the structural story inside the token numbers. Enterprise AI has arrived, and it arrived multimodel. No scaled company is running a single-model production stack. They run one model for coding, another for customer service, another for document summarization, another for cost efficiency at scale. OpenRouter industrialized that pattern.

The investor logic is cleaner than the numbers. The enterprise market already decided to route. That decision was made before the round closed. It shows up in how enterprise CTOs talk about model governance, in how procurement cycles are being structured, in the fact that OpenRouter grew 5x in six months without a major product announcement. The question for Google is not whether routing happens. The question is whether Google has equity in the infrastructure or not. CapitalG bought the inside seat.

NVIDIA's logic is nearly identical. OpenRouter routes queries to inference providers. Some run NVIDIA GPUs. Some run AMD. Some run AWS Trainium or Google TPUs. NVIDIA does not control the routing decision. But NVIDIA now has an equity stake in the company that does. A small hedge against the most consequential variable in AI hardware demand.

The historical precedent is precise. Enterprise software in 1997 required full commitment. Oracle or SAP. One ERP architecture. One vendor relationship. By 2005, systems integrators had built abstraction layers. Enterprises ran Oracle in finance and SAP in supply chain without committing to one stack. Those middleware companies captured margin from both vendors.

ERP vendors funded the middleware. Then integrated it. Then acquired it.

The model race is not competing with the routing layer. Every new Anthropic release, every new Gemini version, every new xAI Grok update adds one more option to the catalog. More options means more routing surface. More routing surface means more value.

The labs are competing. OpenRouter is routing.

content_pack.substack_draft:
Most people thought of OpenRouter as a developer tool for comparing model outputs cheaply. The more I looked at the $113 million Series B it just closed, the more I think it might be the most structurally important infrastructure play in the current AI stack.

The investor list is what shifted my view. CapitalG led. NVentures joined. ServiceNow, MongoDB, Snowflake, and Databricks all wrote checks. That is the enterprise software backbone paying to be inside the thing that routes traffic away from any individual enterprise software product. That is not hedge-your-bets investing. That is recognizing that the routing layer will capture margin from model providers the same way middleware captured margin from ERP vendors in the late 1990s.

The number that surprised me most: 25 trillion tokens per week, up 5 times in six months. Over a quadrillion tokens a year already flowing through a platform that barely existed at meaningful scale eighteen months ago. Enterprises are not debating whether to use multiple models. They already are. OpenRouter just industrialized the pattern.

What I am less sure about is whether the neutral position holds as the model providers start doing their own routing, governance, and pricing. Google could preferentially route Gemini queries through its own API. OpenAI could bundle routing into its enterprise tier. The routing layer is structurally valuable now because it is neutral. Whether it stays neutral as the labs respond to losing wallet share is the part I would want to watch closely over the next twelve months.

ideas.title: Tech Buyouts Collapsed 82% in Two Months. The DCF Model Broke.
ideas.trend: Axios reported tech PE is 'frozen' on May 20; PitchBook data shows global tech buyout value was $9.3B in April and May combined vs $52.6B in March alone — an 82% collapse in deal activity
ideas.consensus: PE is exercising caution because of AI uncertainty, macro headwinds, and Gulf conflict overhang
ideas.angle: This is not sentiment-driven caution. This is a valuation methodology failure. PE's buyout model requires confident year-5 to year-7 cash flow projections. AI disruption makes those projections impossible for software companies today. When terminal value becomes unknowable, deals do not price slowly — they do not price at all. And paradoxically, the same AI compression that drove software to historic multiple lows is the reason PE cannot step in at the compressed prices.
ideas.pillar: PE vs public markets / SaaS-AI bifurcation

content_pack.x_longform:
The one thing that freezes a private equity deal is an unfinishable DCF model.

Per Axios reporting this week, global tech buyout value totaled $9.3 billion across April and May combined. March alone produced $52.6 billion. Per PitchBook, that is an 82% collapse in deal activity across two months.

The standard explanation is caution. AI uncertainty. Gulf conflict overhang. Interest rate sensitivity. All of that is real and also incomplete.

The real problem is terminal value.

A standard leveraged buyout model projects cash flows over seven years. Years one and two are modeled off current customer lists, current churn, current contract structures. Investors can stress-test those numbers. Years five and six require assumptions about competitive position. For software companies, competitive position in 2031 requires a view on what GPT-9 or Claude 7 can replace, automate, or eliminate.

Nobody has that view. So nobody can finish the model. When the model cannot be finished, the deal cannot price. When the deal cannot price, it does not close.

Software is now trading below the S&P 500 forward multiple for the first time in modern market history, per SaaStr data. That repricing happened in public markets. Public markets can express uncertainty in a price. PE cannot. PE builds models. When the model breaks, the deal freezes.

The structural irony: the same AI transformation that compressed public software multiples is also why PE cannot step in at compressed prices. PE historically cleans up valuation dislocations. It buys at lows that public sentiment created. This is exactly such a dislocation. And PE is sitting on the sideline.

That will not last. Eventually someone builds an LBO model structured around AI uncertainty rather than pretending to project through it. Shorter hold periods. Carve-outs that isolate AI-exposed revenue from AI-resilient revenue. Explicit pricing of the optionality of a business's AI transition rather than burying it in the terminal growth rate.

The first PE firm that figures out how to finish the DCF for AI-disrupted software will have no competition. Every other buyer is frozen.

Public markets can bet on uncertainty. PE needs to model it. Right now, the models are not finishing.

content_pack.substack_draft:
$9.3 billion. That is how much global tech buyout activity happened across April and May combined. That number is doing a lot of work in this story.

March alone produced $52.6 billion. The comparison is per PitchBook, cited in Axios reporting this week. In two months, tech buyout activity fell 82%. Axios called it a freeze, and that word feels right.

The conventional explanation is uncertainty, AI disruption, Gulf conflict overhang, interest rate sensitivity. All of that is real. What is also real, and less discussed, is that the standard PE buyout model is breaking on a specific input: terminal value. A leveraged buyout needs projected cash flows across 7 years. Years one and two can be modeled from current customer data. Years five and six require assumptions about competitive position in 2031. For software companies, that requires a view on what AI agents will automate or eliminate between now and then. Nobody has a confident view on that. When the terminal value cannot be filled in, the model does not finish. When the model does not finish, the deal does not price.

I keep coming back to the structural trap: the same AI compression that drove software multiples to historic lows, below the S&P 500 for the first time, is also the reason PE cannot step in at those prices. The buyer that historically cleaned up these dislocations cannot price this one. Whether that resolves through shorter hold structures, AI-adjusted carve-outs, or one firm that publishes a new methodology for pricing AI-disrupted businesses is the question I do not have an answer to yet.

ideas.title: Baidu's AI Revenue Crossed 50%. Zero NVIDIA Chips.
ideas.trend: Baidu Q1 2026 earnings announced May 18: AI revenue exceeded 50% of core business for first time; AI Cloud up 79% YoY; GPU Cloud up 184% YoY; all workloads running on Huawei Ascend hardware
ideas.consensus: Chinese AI development is constrained by US export controls that block access to NVIDIA's best hardware
ideas.angle: The company US export controls were specifically designed to handicap just crossed the AI-majority revenue milestone running entirely on domestic chips. The embargo created the captive procurement relationship that forced Huawei to accelerate Ascend development. Baidu needed domestic chips to survive; Huawei needed a serious anchor customer. The constraint became the development contract.

content_pack.x_longform:
The company US export controls were designed to handicap just crossed the AI-majority revenue mark. Without a single NVIDIA chip.

Baidu's Q1 2026 results: AI revenue above 50% of core business for the first time. AI Cloud up 79% year over year. GPU Cloud up 184%. Every chip powering those numbers: Huawei Ascend.

The chip embargo created the procurement relationship that forced Huawei to accelerate. Baidu needed domestic chips to survive. Huawei needed a serious anchor customer to justify the Ascend investment. The constraint became the development contract.

You cannot embargo a pivot.

content_pack.substack_draft:
The export controls narrative runs like this: cut off NVIDIA chips, slow the AI development. Baidu's Q1 2026 numbers suggest the second step did not follow from the first.

Baidu reported AI revenue above 50% of its core business for the first time in that quarter. AI Cloud grew 79% year over year. GPU Cloud grew 184%. Every chip running those workloads is Huawei Ascend. The US Entity List had blocked Baidu's access to H100 and H200 hardware in early 2025.

What the export controls actually produced was a committed procurement relationship. Baidu needed a viable domestic chip stack to continue operating at scale. Huawei needed a large, serious customer to accelerate Ascend development. That symbiosis, forced by the embargo, built a chip stack now credible enough to run triple-digit cloud growth.

I want to be careful not to overclaim this. The Ascend stack is still behind NVIDIA's best hardware on raw performance per watt. The gap is real. But Baidu's numbers suggest the gap is already small enough for production inference and cloud deployment. Whether it closes enough for frontier training is still genuinely open. What is no longer open is whether the embargo slowed Baidu's AI pivot. The Q1 numbers answered that.
